newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: EU, southern Africa talk peace, but no promises.
newsitem.headline: EU, southern Africa talk peace, but no promises.

text.p: European Union and southern African foreign ministers ended two days of talks on political and economic cooperation on Tuesday with few new words and little promise of action to end conflicts in Africa.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said the ministers from Europe and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) discussed the peace process in Angola and the conflict in Burundi, but little new was agreed.

"(It) was agreed the process towards peace must be expedited," he told a news conference when asked about a closing communique which made sweeping reference to the two countries which dominated the topic of conflict resolution.
Mozambican Foreign Minister Leonardo Simao added that the participants had agreed to support "current programmes".
Spring said ministers did not formally discuss a U.S. proposed all-Africa rapid deployment force to deal with conflicts around the continent.
"It was not formally raised because both our organisations have not formally discussed the subject," he said of the proposed force.

SADC executive secretary Kaire Mbuende earlier said most countries in the region had strong reservations about the proposal and British Overseas Development Minister Lynda Chalker said participants had discussed other priorities.
"It did not arise, I think, because we have enough to deal with in southern Africa. It may have arisen on the sidelines, but I am not aware of that," she told Reuters.
The SADC comprises Angola, Botswana, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Lesotho, Tanzania, South Africa, Swaziland, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Delegates to the conference postponed a decision on an EU offer to help clear an estimated 20 million landmines mines in southern Africa, many left from years of civil war in Angola and Mozambique.
The proposal would have to be discussed further before it might be adopted, the ministers agreed.

The communique also said other new programmes would only be discussed after countries had consolidated agreements from the first EU-SADC foreign ministers' meeting two years ago. Those agreements covered such matters as strengthening democracy and promoting trade.
Spring said the EU had reassured SADC states worried about a possible free trade agreement between the region's economic giant South Africa and Europe.
An agreement would not compromise the interests of South Africa's neighbours, he said.
